terms.gloss: be broke, be unable to pay
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.10.3: solvendō nōn erat (Lewis & Short s.v. solvō)
terms.comment: A dative of the gerund: “not to be up to paying”. Latin says it with a verb phrase, not an adjective.

terms.gloss: not have a penny: be broke
evidence: Plaut. Epid. 330: is nummum nūllum habēs
terms.comment: What a person says of himself; solvendō nōn esse is to be unable to pay one’s debts, of a man or a city.

phrases.latin: cēnābis bene; nam tuī Catullī plēnus sacculus est arāneārum.
phrases.english: you’ll dine well; for your Catullus’s purse is full of cobwebs.

phrases.latin: quī, tibi quoi dīvitiae domī maxumae sunt, is nummum nūllum habēs
phrases.english: you, who have the greatest riches at home, haven’t a penny

phrases.latin: Nūllus mihi nummus superest; omnia in librōs impendī.
phrases.english: I’ve run out of money; I spent it all on books.

sources: Lewis & Short: solvo · Lewis & Short: nummus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 94.
